stemMd:
In the 1950s the province of Merrin paid farmers to plant hedges along their fields as windbreaks to keep soil from blowing away. Farm records show that hedges were planted on almost every enrolled farm, and officials declared the program a success. Economist Halvard Quist notes, however, that payments were made on proof of planting, not on proof that the hedges survived, and aerial photographs taken ten years later show that fewer than a third of the hedges were still standing. Once they had been paid, Quist found, farmers had little reason to spend scarce water keeping young hedges alive through their first dry summer. Quist does not conclude that paying for windbreaks is wasteful; he argues that what the program rewarded determined what it achieved.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

options.label: A
options.textMd: Quist shows that Merrin's officials exaggerated the number of hedges that farmers had planted under the program.

options.label: B
options.textMd: Quist finds that most of the hedges died because Merrin's dry summers made the province unsuited to growing windbreaks.

options.label: C
options.textMd: Quist argues that the Merrin program left few lasting hedges because it paid farmers for planting rather than for survival.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Quist argues that paying farmers to plant hedges is an ineffective way to protect farmland from wind erosion.

explanationMd:
When a text ends by stating what its central figure does **and does not** conclude, that final sentence sets the boundaries of the main idea. Quist does not say windbreak payments are wasteful; he says "what the program rewarded determined what it achieved." Unpack that with the details: the program paid on proof of planting, so hedges were planted almost everywhere; it did not pay for survival, so farmers had no reason to water them, and fewer than a third survived ten years.

The choice saying that the program left few lasting hedges because it paid for planting rather than for survival states the claim and its cause in concrete terms.

Two wrong answers are built from real details. Dry summers are mentioned, but only as the reason watering cost farmers something; Quist's explanation is the incentive, not the climate. And the claim that paying for hedges is ineffective is exactly the conclusion the last sentence says Quist does not draw. A quick check for any main-idea choice: would the author of the text sign it? Quist would reject both.

distractorRationale.d: This is the conclusion the final sentence explicitly says Quist does not reach. His point is that the program's design, not the idea of paying for windbreaks, produced the poor result.
distractorRationale.a: The text accepts that the hedges were planted: farm records show planting on almost every enrolled farm. The problem Quist identifies is that most planted hedges later died, not that the planting figures were inflated.
distractorRationale.b: Dry summers appear in the text only as the reason that keeping young hedges alive took scarce water. Quist attributes the losses to farmers having no incentive to supply that water once paid, not to the province being unsuitable for hedges.

accessibilityText: A short economics passage. In the 1950s the province of Merrin paid farmers to plant hedges as windbreaks. Farm records show hedges were planted on almost every enrolled farm, and officials called the program a success. Economist Halvard Quist notes that payments were made on proof of planting, not proof of survival, and aerial photographs ten years later show fewer than a third of the hedges still standing. Once paid, farmers had little reason to spend scarce water keeping young hedges alive through their first dry summer. Quist does not conclude that paying for windbreaks is wasteful; he argues that what the program rewarded determined what it achieved. The question asks for the main idea. The choices are: Quist shows that officials exaggerated the number of hedges planted; Quist finds that most hedges died because Merrin's dry summers made the province unsuited to windbreaks; Quist argues that the program left few lasting hedges because it paid for planting rather than for survival; and Quist argues that paying farmers to plant hedges is an ineffective way to protect farmland from wind erosion.

provenance.notes: Original main-idea item. Merrin, its windbreak program and Quist's analysis are invented. The two strongest distractors are the conclusion the text says Quist rejects and a cause built from a background detail.

review.author: sat-wave8-rw-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: Quist's point is that paying on proof of planting rather than survival led to few surviving hedges ('what the program rewarded determined what it achieved'). The text says hedges were planted, not that numbers were exaggerated; the climate-unsuitability reading misplaces the cause (farmers chose not to water); 'paying is ineffective' is explicitly denied. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave8-sat-rw-run1) reached the same answer: Quist's point is that paying for planting rather than survival is why fewer than a third of hedges remained. Officials did not exaggerate planting counts (records show planting occurred); dry summers are not blamed as making the province unsuitable; the text explicitly says he does not conclude paying for windbreaks is wasteful.]
